How Ethereum works

You open a wallet, type an amount and press Send. About twelve seconds later the money has moved. A quarter of an hour after that it is final: moving it back would mean destroying billions of dollars of other people's deposits. No bank did this, and no company's computer. The machine that did it is called Ethereum, and it is run by thousands of strangers who do not trust one another.

Here is a small one, working. Alice and Bob each have an account. Press the button to send 1 ether from Alice to Bob and follow the transaction: it waits in a pool with other people's, a validator, one of the participants who keep the chain going, puts it into a block, other validators vote for that block, and a few blocks later it is locked:

Every part of that picture is doing a job, and more went on behind it than it shows. Something made sure that only Alice could spend Alice's ether. Something chose one order for everybody's transactions. Something worked out the new balances, identically on every computer, charged a fee and destroyed most of it. Something chose who makes each block, and something declared, at a definite moment, that a block was final.

This page builds that machine from nothing. We start with a ledger that barely works and add one part each time it breaks, until it is the Ethereum of November 2026. On the way we open the boxes that are usually left shut: how a signature proves anything, what is inside a hash, how tens of thousands of votes fit into one signature.

I assume you can program, and that hashes, signatures and a chain of blocks are at least familiar words. Everything else is here. One thing is not: nothing on this page is advice to buy, hold or stake anything.

The small chain above has 12 validators and room for 30 transfers in a block. The real one has about 785,000 validators and room for a few thousand. Before either, we need something much simpler: a table of who owns what, and three computers that each keep a copy.

One ledger, many copies

Take a table with three rows: Alice has 10 ether (ETH for short, on the figures), Bob has 2, Carol has 5. A bank would keep this table on its own computer, and everyone would have to trust the bank. We want nobody in charge, so every computer that takes part keeps its own copy. I'll call each of those computers a node, the table the ledger, and a message that changes it, such as "Alice pays Bob 1", a payment.

In the demonstration below three nodes each hold the ledger. Press a button to make a payment. It travels from node to node, and each node applies it to its own copy. Under each node is a short hash of its copy, so that three ledgers can be compared at a glance:

The hashes match again after every payment. The reason is the idea that the rest of this page defends: nodes that start from the same ledger and apply the same payments in the same order end with the same ledger. They never send each other the table. They only need the same payments, in the same order.

Who may write

Nothing so far stops a node from inventing a payment. One of the nodes below belongs to an attacker, who has a row of its own. Forge a payment from Alice to the attacker and watch every node obey. Then switch on the check and forge again:

With the check on, a payment counts only if it carries a signature: a seal that can be made only with the payer's private key, and that anyone can test against the payer's public key. You have met signatures as a tool. For now this one stays a sealed box; the next section opens it. The forged payment has no valid seal, so each node refuses it by itself, without asking anybody.

A valid seal has a weakness: it stays valid. Bob has received Alice's signed payment of 1 ether and kept the bytes. Nothing stops him from sending the same bytes again, and again:

Every replay passes the check, because the signature really is Alice's, and each one costs her another ether. The cure is a counter. Switch it on and replay once more: each account now remembers how many payments it has sent, and each payment says which one it is. A node applies a payment only if the two numbers agree, and then adds one to the account's. That counter is the account's nonce. The replay says "payment number 0", the account is already at 1, and the node refuses.

In what order

One hole is left, and it is the deep one. Alice has 10 ether and signs two payments, both numbered 0: 8 to Bob and 8 to Carol. Each is valid by itself. She hands one to the node on the left and the other to the node on the right. Send both, and use the slider to change which of them reaches the middle node first:

Every node did the right thing. It applied the first payment it heard and refused the second, whose number was already used. But the nodes did not hear them in the same order, so their ledgers now differ, and no rule we have says which one is correct. Signatures and nonces settle who may write. They are silent about whose write came first.

Settling the order takes blocks and a lottery, and we will get there. First I owe you the inside of the two sealed boxes this section leaned on: the signature, and the hash under each node.

Inside a signature

A signature has to do something that sounds impossible. It must convince a stranger that Alice approved one particular payment, and it must be made with a key that the stranger never sees and cannot work out. The trick is a kind of multiplication that is easy to do and hopeless to undo. To get to it we need arithmetic in which numbers wrap around.

This section and the next open two boxes that the rest of the page uses only from the outside. If you would rather leave them shut, skip ahead to "A lottery for the next block". Two later passages, on combining signatures and on commitments to blobs, lean on the curve points introduced here, and say so where they do.

Numbers on a ring

Put the numbers 0 to 16 on a ring. To add or multiply, do it the usual way and then keep only the remainder after dividing by 17. This is arithmetic modulo 17. The demonstration below multiplies two numbers this way and also looks for each number's inverse: the number you multiply it by to get 1. Move the sliders, then change the modulus to 18:

Modulo 17 every number except 0 has an inverse, so you can divide by anything: dividing is multiplying by the inverse. Modulo 18 that fails. Twice anything is even, and an even number never leaves a remainder of 1 when divided by 18, so 2 has no inverse. The trouble is that 18 has factors, and 17, a prime, has none. Arithmetic modulo a prime, where all four operations work and every answer is one of a fixed set of whole numbers, is called a finite field. Everything in this section happens in one.

A curve of thirty points

Now take the equation y² = x³ + 7 and ask for which whole numbers x and y, each from 0 to 42, it holds modulo 43. Below, every solution is drawn as a point. Use the slider to walk across the columns:

There are 30 points. A column has either none or two, and the two are mirror images, because if y works then so does 43 − y. Mathematicians call this scatter an elliptic curve. Over ordinary numbers the same equation is a smooth line, which is why it is called a curve. The smooth picture is only a memory aid. The real thing is the scatter.

What makes these points useful is that they can be added. The recipe is fixed: draw the line through two points P and Q, find the third point where it meets the curve, and take that point's mirror image. All of it is done modulo 43, so the "line" wraps around the edges. The sliders name each point as a multiple of one starting point, G, which the next figure explains. Pick any two points:

The sum of two points of the curve is always a point of the curve. Adding a point to itself uses the tangent in place of the line through two points. And a point plus its mirror image gives a line straight up that meets nothing: the answer is defined to be one extra point, written O and called the point at infinity. O behaves like zero: adding it changes nothing. With O the curve has 31 points in all.

Easy one way

If points can be added, a point can be multiplied by a number: 5·G means G + G + G + G + G. Fix one point, G = (2, 12). Since doubling is cheap, n·G never needs n additions: double repeatedly, and add G in at the right moments. Choose n with the slider and watch the path, then press Find n to go the other way:

Forward takes a handful of steps. Backward, from the point to n, the demonstration can only try G, 2·G, 3·G and so on. Among 31 points that is a moment's work. Ethereum uses the same equation modulo a prime close to 2²⁵⁶, a curve named secp256k1. There, forward is about 256 doublings. Backward, there are cleverer methods than trying one by one, but the best of them still needs about 2¹²⁸ steps, which is out of reach.

One detail for what follows. Adding G to itself 31 times arrives at O, and after that the multiples repeat. So the multiplier of a point only matters modulo 31, while the coordinates of points are worked modulo 43. Two different wrap-arounds are in play, and I will say which one I mean.

That gap between forward and backward is the lock. Alice picks a number and tells nobody: her private key. Hers will be 7. She publishes 7·G, which is the point (25, 18): her public key. Anyone can see the point. Nobody can get back to the 7.

Signing

To sign, Alice must show that she knows the 7 without revealing it. The scheme Ethereum uses is called ECDSA. Step through it below. The message is represented by a number, its hash, here 11 (the next section explains hashes). Alice also picks a second secret: a fresh number k, used for this one signature and never again:

The signature is two numbers. The first, r, is the x coordinate of the point k·G. The second, s, is the hash plus r times the private key, divided by k, all modulo 31. The checker never learns the private key or k. It divides the hash by s and r by s, and uses the two results as multipliers: the first times G, plus the second times Alice's public key. It accepts the signature if the x coordinate of the point it gets is r.

Why does that land on k·G? Her public key is 7·G, so the checker's point is G multiplied by (hash + r × 7) ÷ s. And s was built so that this is exactly k. The 7 was needed to build s. It is not needed to check it, and someone without it cannot find an s that makes the two points agree. Change the message hash to 12 and the checker's point lands somewhere else: the signature fits one message only.

There is a bonus. The same arithmetic can be run backwards, from the signature to the public key. Given only the message hash 11 and the signature (29, 15), try both settings of the switch:

Two points of the curve have x = 29, and each leads to a different public key: (25, 18), which is Alice's, or (21, 18), which is nobody's. So a signature carries one extra bit, called v, saying which point was meant. With it, the signature alone identifies its signer. This is why an Ethereum transaction has no field saying who sent it. The sender is whoever's key comes out.

The number that must never repeat

The fresh secret k looks like a detail. It is not. Below, Alice has signed two different messages and used k = 6 for both. Press Solve:

Both signatures begin with the same r, which gives the repeat away, and two lines of school algebra on public numbers then produce k and after it the private key. With a fresh k the algebra has nothing to hold on to. This has happened for real. In 2010 the key that Sony used to sign PlayStation 3 software was recovered because k was a constant, and in 2013 a faulty random-number generator on Android phones cost Bitcoin wallet users their funds. Wallets now derive k from the message and the key, so that it cannot repeat by accident.

A real private key is 32 bytes, a real signature is 65 bytes, and everything else is as you have just seen it. One thing was skipped: the "message hash". Alice does not sign the payment. She signs a short number that stands for it, and her address turns out to be made the same way.

Inside a hash

A hash function takes any amount of data and returns a short, fixed-size number that stands for it, its digest. Signing the digest is safe only if nobody can find two different messages with the same digest, or a message to fit a given digest. Ethereum's hash function is called Keccak-256, and it works like a sponge.

The sponge is a row of 200 bytes, all zero to begin with. The message is cut into pieces of 136 bytes, and the last piece is filled out to full length. Each piece is mixed into the first 136 bytes of the sponge, and then the whole sponge is stirred. When the message is used up, the first 32 bytes of the sponge are the digest. Step through it, and try the longer messages:

However long the message, the sponge stays 200 bytes and the digest 32. The last 64 bytes of the sponge are never written to directly and never read out; they carry what has been absorbed so far from one stirring to the next. One more thing: switch the filler to that of SHA-3, the standard that grew out of Keccak. A single filler byte differs, and the digest is a completely different number. Ethereum adopted Keccak before the standard was finished, so a library's "SHA3-256" gives different answers from Ethereum's hash.

The stirring

All the strength is in the stirring. The 200 bytes are treated as 1,600 bits, arranged as 25 lanes of 64 bits. One round of stirring is five simple moves, and a full stir is 24 rounds. Below is the sponge just after a short word has been mixed in. Step through one round:

Four of the five moves, the first three and the last, only shuffle bits or combine them with XOR: mix each bit with bits from the lanes beside it, rotate each lane, move the lanes around, add a constant. Moves like those alone could be undone by solving simple equations. The exception is the fourth move, which combines each bit with two others using AND and NOT. One such step per round, repeated 24 times, is what leaves no known way to work the result backwards. Run all 24 rounds and the few set bits become noise.

How good is the noise? Here is a message as 128 bits and its digest as 256. Tap any bit of the message to flip it, or flip one at random, and count how many bits of the digest change:

About half of them, every time: a digest that differs in one bit of input is as different as an unrelated one. Nothing about the message can be read from the digest, and no small change produces a small change. The slider shows where this comes from. With one round the flipped bit has reached only a few places. By three or four rounds it has reached everywhere. That alone is not security: versions cut down to a handful of rounds have been broken, and the full 24 leave a wide margin.

An address

Ethereum hashes nearly everything: transactions, blocks, code, the tables you will meet later. (Some later parts of Ethereum use an older standard function, SHA-256, for the same job.) The first use is the name of an account. Step through how an account's address is made:

Take the 64 bytes of the public key, hash them, keep the last 20 bytes. That is all. Nobody registers an address or asks permission for one: pick another private key and its address already exists, in the sense that anyone can send ether to it. Because recovering a public key from a signature leads straight to an address, a node that checks a transaction's signature learns which account sent it. The capital letters are a checksum made, again, with a hash, so that a mistyped address is almost always caught.

Keys, signatures and hashes now settle who may change the ledger. The other hole from the first section is still open: two honest nodes can hear two valid payments in different orders.

A lottery for the next block

The nodes need one order for everybody's payments. This section shows how Ethereum got one from 2015 to 2022. The method has since been retired, but what replaced it makes sense only against it. Start by not ordering payments one at a time. Collect payments into a batch, fix their order inside it, and add one more field: the hash of the batch before it, its parent. Such a batch is a block, and the hash is the link that turns blocks into a chain. Below are five. Pick one, change a payment in it, and watch the links:

The edited block has a new hash, so the next block, which names the old one, no longer points at it, and every block after that is cut loose too. A change anywhere shows everywhere after it. But try the second button: recompute the later hashes, and the chain is whole again with the forgery inside. Hashes alone only help someone who remembers the old ones. To make rewriting hard, adding a block has to cost something.

Work as a lottery ticket

The cost is a puzzle with no shortcut. A block counts only if its hash, read as a number, falls below a threshold. The only way to get there is to try: put a number in the block, hash, look, change the number, hash again. (That number is also called a nonce. It has nothing to do with an account's.) Whoever does this is a miner, and the scheme is proof of work.

The miner who finds such a hash has made the next block, and is paid for it in newly created ether: the block reward, 5 ether at first and 2 in the last years. The order of payments inside the block is the order for everyone. If it holds Alice's payment to Bob, her payment to Carol is refused everywhere as a used nonce. Each dot below is one try:

A lower line means more tries per block on average, and that average is the difficulty. Now look at the histogram of waits. Most blocks come sooner than the average, and a few take several times as long. Every try is a fresh draw, and failures buy nothing. So a miner with a tenth of all the hash power, meaning a tenth of all the tries made per second, finds about a tenth of the blocks, and nobody can say which ones in advance.

For scale: in May 2022 Ethereum's miners together made about 1.1 × 10¹⁵ tries a second, and a block took about 1.4 × 10¹⁶ of them, or thirteen seconds.

Ethereum's miners did not use a bare hash. Bitcoin's puzzle had been taken over by chips built for nothing else, and Ethereum's designers wanted ordinary graphics cards to stay in the game. Their puzzle, Ethash, makes every try read from a large dataset. Step through one try:

A real try makes 64 jumps into a dataset that began at 1 gigabyte in 2015 and had grown to about 5 by 2022. Each jump depends on what the last one read, so the whole dataset has to sit in fast memory. A node that only checks a block needs none of that: it rebuilds the few items it wants from a far smaller cache, 16 megabytes at the start. A miner could work from the cache too, at many times the effort per try, so mining is only competitive with the whole dataset in memory. Hard to produce, cheap to check.

The dataset was meant to keep out chips built only for mining, which are fast at hashing and poor at holding gigabytes of memory. That hope did not hold. A chip built for Ethash was announced in April 2018.

Keeping the pace

Miners come and go, and hardware improves. With a fixed threshold, blocks would come faster every year. So the difficulty adjusts itself at every block: a little up if the block came less than 10 seconds after its parent, a little down if it took 20 or more. Change the miners' hash power and watch it respond:

When hash power doubles, blocks come twice as fast for a while, and the difficulty climbs by a two-thousandth per block until the gaps are back near 14 seconds. No constant anywhere says "14 seconds". It is simply where this rule balances. (This is the rule of 2016 and 2017. A later variant used 9 seconds and one more input, and balanced nearer 13.) Ethereum's blocks did arrive 13 to 14.5 seconds apart for most of seven years. Bitcoin aims for ten minutes.

The price of short blocks

Why not one second, then? Because a new block takes time to reach every miner, and until it does, the others are still working on top of the old one. Below, a found block spreads as a ring that takes about 12 seconds to reach a miner, about what Bitcoin's network needed in 2013. Shorten the time between blocks:

At ten minutes, a second block inside those 12 seconds is rare: about 2 in a hundred. At 12 seconds the figure counts about two blocks in five. Of two blocks at the same position in the chain only one can stay. The other is stale, and the work in it protected nothing. It is also unfair: a large group of miners never races against its own blocks, so stale blocks hurt small miners most and push everyone toward the biggest group.

Ethereum's answer was to pay for stale blocks. A later block may name up to two of them as its uncles, and then both miners earn something. Move the slider to change how late the uncle is named:

An uncle named by the very next block earns seven eighths of a full reward. Each block of delay costs another eighth, and after six it earns nothing. The bars show what this bought in one simulation with 12-second blocks: a group with a quarter of the hash power earned 18% more than its share without uncle pay, and about 2.5% more with it.

On the real network, with blocks 13 to 14 seconds apart, between 4 and 11 uncles were named for every hundred blocks in most years, and many more during the crush of late 2017 and 2018, up to 39 on one day. In ordinary times that is far fewer than the ring above would predict, which suggests that real blocks crossed the network much faster than my 12 seconds.

Never final

Two blocks at the same position mean the chain has forked, and nodes need a rule for choosing a branch. The rule was: follow the branch with the most work in it, the greatest total difficulty. Honest miners build on that branch, so it pulls ahead and the other is forgotten. But the rule does not care who did the work. Below, a merchant is paid in one block, waits until six more have been built on it, and hands over the goods. Meanwhile an attacker mines a branch in secret:

With 30% of the hash power the attacker seldom catches up, and waiting for more blocks makes a success rarer, never impossible. Give it more than half and watch one attack through. The merchant sees the payment buried under six blocks and hands over the goods. Then a heavier branch appears in which the payment never happened, and every node switches to it, exactly as the rule demands. With more than half, the attacker always wins in the end.

This has happened. Ethereum Classic, a smaller chain that used the same puzzle, was rewritten thousands of blocks deep three times in August 2020. In the first of those attacks, hash power rented for about 192,000 dollars took about 5.6 million.

Proof of work gave the nodes their one order, and it ran Ethereum from 2015 to 2022. It left two debts: the electricity behind all those tries, and blocks that are only ever probably settled. Both are paid later on this page. First, a block so far carries only payments. What else could it carry?

Accounts instead of coins

So far the ledger has been a table of balances, and all a payment could say was "pay". Before giving it more to say, look at how Bitcoin keeps its books, because one of Ethereum's earliest decisions was to keep them differently. Bitcoin has no table of balances. It has coins: each records an amount and who may spend it, and spending a coin destroys it and creates new ones. Watch one payment in both systems, then make it again:

On the left, Alice's coin of 10 became 1 for Bob and 9 in change, and the second payment destroyed the 9 in turn. Her balance is whatever her coins add up to at the moment. On the right, two balances changed, and Alice's nonce counted the payment.

Ethereum's designers chose the right-hand way for several reasons: it takes less space, it is simpler to write programs against, and an account always sits at the same place, which a later section relies on. Bitcoin's coins carry tiny scripts, and Ethereum's founding paper lists what those cannot do: they cannot loop, cannot remember anything except "spent" or "unspent", and cannot see the amounts they guard or the chain they live on.

Here is an Ethereum account, opened up:

Every account has the same four fields. The nonce is the counter from the first section. The balance is kept as a whole number of wei, the smallest unit: one ether is 10¹⁸ wei. Fees will be quoted in gwei, a billionth of an ether. The other two fields are hashes that stand for a program and its data, and they are empty for Alice. They are filled in for a second kind of account, the subject of the next section. All the accounts together are the state, and from here on that word replaces "ledger".

A transaction, exactly

What changes the state is a transaction: a signed message from an account. The payments of the earlier sections were the simplest kind. One that only moves ether I'll call a transfer. Here is Alice's transfer of 1 ether to Bob, both as the short list of numbers it is and as the bytes that travel between nodes:

The whole transaction is a little over a hundred bytes. The list is packed into bytes, the bytes are hashed with Keccak-256, and the digest is what Alice signs; the three numbers of her signature are attached. Look for the sender: there is none. As we saw, the signature gives it away. The chain number keeps a transaction signed for one network from being replayed on another. Three fields are about gas and fees. Leave those for two more sections, and with them the type and the access list, which are bookkeeping.

Every node treats an arriving transaction in the same way. Step through what happens to the transfer:

Recover the sender. Check the nonce. Check that the balance covers the amount plus the largest fee the transaction allows. Then, and only then, change anything. The whole procedure is a function: old state and a transaction go in, a new state comes out. The failing cases, a wrong nonce or too little ether, show the other half of the rule. A transaction that fails a check changes nothing, and cannot be put in a block at all.

This makes a chain of blocks a chain of states. Start from the first state, apply every transaction of every block in order, and you arrive at today's. Any node can do it, and every node that does gets the same answer.

Alice's account uses two of its four fields. The other two are for an account that holds a program.

Code inside an account

With accounts and transfers we have a currency. Any arrangement more complicated than "pay" (pay only if something happened, hold funds for a group, keep a second kind of money) still needs someone trusted to carry it out. Ethereum's founding idea is to let an account carry out rules by itself.

A contract is an account that holds code and has storage of its own. It has no private key, so nobody can sign for it. It does exactly one thing: when a transaction is sent to it, every node runs its code. The simplest contract worth having counts how many times it has been called. Call it a few times:

One transaction, three nodes, three identical runs of the same eight bytes: each node's copy of the counter's storage now holds the same number. Nobody hosts the counter. It lives in every copy of the state, the way a balance does. Alice paid a small fee for each call, and we will come to where that goes.

A contract is born through a transaction too. Step through the creation of the counter:

The transaction named no recipient and carried 17 bytes as its data: a short piece of code that runs once and hands back the 8 bytes to be stored. Nobody chose the new account's address: it is a hash of the creator's address and nonce, so every node computes the same one.

Once the code is stored it stays as it is. No instruction edits it. Whatever those bytes do, they will do the same for everyone from then on. (A contract can be written to hand its work to another contract which its owners may swap, as we will see. The bytes themselves never change.) That is the point of it and, as we are about to see, also the danger.

Money made of storage

A very common kind of contract is a second currency, a token. A token is a table in one contract's storage, holder against amount, and a function that moves amounts between rows. Send some of Alice's:

Look at what changed and what did not. Alice's and Bob's accounts are as they were, apart from her fee and her nonce. Their tokens are two rows in the token contract's storage, and "Alice sends Bob 100 tokens" really means "Alice asks the token contract to edit its table". The transaction's data carries the request: four bytes that name the function, then the recipient, then the amount. Ask for more than she has and the contract's own code refuses. Over two million contracts on Ethereum are tokens of this pattern.

Code is law, until it isn't

Contracts can hold ether, and contracts can call other contracts. Together those allow whole institutions, and one famous kind of mistake. Below is a bank contract. Its withdraw function has three lines: look up the caller's balance, send it, set it to zero. One of its depositors is itself a contract, written by an attacker. Watch the attack, or run it again:

The bank sent the money before it wrote down that the money was gone. Sending ether to a contract runs that contract's code, and the attacker's code used the moment to call withdraw again. The bank looked at its records, found the old balance still there, and paid again, and again. Swap two lines, so that the record is updated first, and the second call finds nothing to take. The mistake is called re-entrancy.

In June 2016 a flaw of this kind, in a more tangled function, let someone drain 3.6 million ether from a contract called The DAO: about a third of what it held. The code had done precisely what it said. After a month of argument the chain's own rules were changed to get the ether back, and about 85% of miners went along. At block 1,920,000, on 20 July 2016, nodes running the new software applied a change to the state that no transaction had asked for. Those who refused kept the old rules, and their chain carried on as Ethereum Classic.

That is what "every node runs the code" can lead to. But run it on what? Thousands of different computers are each expected to get exactly the same answer.

The machine that runs the code

A contract's code cannot be written for any real processor. Nodes run on different chips and different operating systems, and one differing bit in one result would split them. So Ethereum defines a processor of its own, which exists only on paper, and every node runs a program that imitates it. It is the Ethereum Virtual Machine, the EVM.

The EVM has no registers. It works on a stack of 32-byte numbers called words. An instruction takes its inputs off the top of the stack and puts its result back, and each instruction is a single byte, sometimes followed by the bytes it pushes. Step through the smallest program worth running:

The byte 60 means "push the next byte"; 01 means "add the top two". Five bytes, three instructions, and a 5 on the stack. The other programs work the same way. There are about 150 instructions in all, and most are this plain: arithmetic, comparisons, copying and swapping on the stack. A word is 32 bytes because that suits 256-bit cryptography: it is the size of a hash.

The stack is gone when a program ends. What makes a contract a contract is a pair of instructions that reach its permanent storage: one loads a numbered cell, the other stores to it. Here are the eight bytes of the counter. Step through, and keep an eye on the column of prices:

Load cell 0, push a 1, add, store the sum back into cell 0, stop. That is the entire contract. The prices are in a unit called gas, which the next section explains. For now notice how lopsided they are. Adding costs 3. The first touch of a storage cell in a transaction costs 2,100: here, the read. Writing to a cell that was empty costs 20,000 on top. Call it again: changing a cell that already holds something is cheaper, 2,900.

Between stack and storage there is a third place, memory: a scratch pad of bytes for anything too large for the stack. What separates it from storage is how long it lasts. Watch this little program run, then start a new transaction:

Memory came back empty. Storage kept its 7. Storage is part of the state: it sits in every node's copy and will sit there for as long as the chain exists. That is why the first write to storage cost 22,100, which is 2,100 for the first touch and 20,000 for filling an empty cell, where the same write to memory cost 6.

Finding the function

The token contract must do something the counter never had to: find out what its caller wants. The input of a call is a string of bytes, the call data: the bytes we met as the transaction's data. By convention its first four bytes name a function: they are the start of the hash of the function's name and argument types, a9059cbb for the token's function named transfer. Step through the first instructions of the token's code:

Load the call data, shift away all but its first four bytes, compare with the constant, and jump. A jump sets the position in the program, and it is how the EVM does both "if" and loops. Call a function the contract does not have and nothing matches: the code falls through to an instruction that cancels the call.

Here is that function itself, the machinery behind the table of the previous section:

The table turns out to be made of hashes. Storage is only numbered cells, so the code keeps each holder's amount in a cell whose number is a hash made from the holder's address. To move tokens it hashes Alice's address, loads that cell, checks she has enough, subtracts and stores; then does the same for Bob with an addition. Two reads and two writes, and almost all of the cost is in them.

Calls inside calls

A contract can call another contract in the middle of its own run. The called code gets a fresh frame: a stack and memory of its own. Step through one call, then change its kind:

In an ordinary call, B's code runs on B's storage, and B sees A as its caller. If B fails, B's changes are rolled back and A is told with a 0 on its stack; A can carry on. The careless bank worked this way, and the attacker's contract was the B that called back. The delegate call is the odd one: B's code, running on A's storage. Contracts use it to borrow code they do not want to carry themselves.

The same answer everywhere

Now the reason for all this austerity. Below, three nodes run one transaction whose code stores "the time now". Run it, then change what the code is allowed to read:

Reading each node's own clock, three nodes stored three numbers. Their states no longer match, and the chain has split over one transaction. With the timestamp written in the block they agree, because the block is the same for all of them. This is why the EVM has no clock, no random numbers, no files, no network and no fractions that might round differently. A program sees the transaction, the state and a few fields of the block, and nothing else. Given those, its result is fixed: it is deterministic.

One danger remains in the design. The EVM has jumps, so it has loops, and a loop does not have to end.

Every step has a price

Here is a contract of three bytes: mark this spot, push a zero, jump to position zero. It jumps back to its own start for ever. Every node that receives a transaction calling it has to run it, and no node can know beforehand that it never stops, because there is no general way to tell whether a program halts. Send that transaction:

With no limit, every node is stuck on one transaction and nothing behind it moves. One sender has stopped the network, for free. The fix is to charge for every instruction. Switch the charge on and send again. The transaction now states how much gas it is prepared to use, its gas limit. Each turn of the loop takes 11 from it, and when nothing is left the run stops, whatever it was doing. The loop still wasted the nodes' time, but a bounded amount of it, and the sender paid for all of it.

A meter

Gas is a count of work, not an amount of money. What a unit costs in ether is the next section's subject. Here is the call to the counter again, with its meter. Step through it:

The first 21,000 is charged to every transaction, for checking its signature and keeping the books. Then each instruction takes its price. With a limit of 50,000 the call finishes with gas to spare, and the spare is handed back: Alice pays for 43,110.

Now lower the limit to 40,000. The meter cannot cover the write to storage, and the call stops, out of gas. Cell 0 keeps its old value, as if nothing had been called, except that Alice pays for all 40,000. The nodes did the work, and work is what is charged. Notice the difference from a transaction with a wrong nonce, which cannot enter a block at all. This one enters, runs, fails and pays.

What things cost

Each price is meant to follow what the step costs a node. Here is the list:

The scale is logarithmic because it has to be. Arithmetic costs 3 to 5. Hashing costs a few dozen. Touching a storage cell for the first time in a transaction costs 2,100, since the node must fetch it from its database. Filling an empty cell costs 20,000 more, 22,100 in all, since every node will keep those 32 bytes for as long as the chain exists. Gas mostly measures touching the state and making it bigger, not computing.

A token transfer shows it: nearly all of its roughly 48,900 gas is the flat 21,000 plus two reads and two writes. On the real chain, moving the largest dollar-pegged token takes about 46,000 gas, and a trade on an exchange that is itself a contract about 117,000.

A wrong price is dangerous. In September 2016 someone noticed that an instruction which makes a node look up another account on disk cost only 20 gas. A block may hold only so much gas in total (we come to that limit in a moment), so the cheaper an instruction is, the more of it fits into one block. Here is a block filled with that instruction:

At 20 gas one block could force about 50,000 disk reads, and nodes needed 20 to 60 seconds to check a block when blocks were arriving every 14. For about a month the network limped, and miners shrank their blocks to a tenth of the usual size to cope. The cure was two emergency upgrades, the first of which raised the price to 700. Reads of the state have been raised again since, to 2,600 for the first touch of an account. Prices are not constants of nature. They are corrected when the hardware or the size of the state changes.

How much fits

One more number: the size of a block. It is not set in bytes or in transactions but in gas, as the block gas limit. Move it:

At today's 60 million a block could hold 2,857 plain transfers, which is 238 a second at today's pace of one block every 12 seconds. The chain in fact carries about 22 a second: blocks run about half full, for a reason the next section gives, and the average transaction does the work of five and a half transfers.

Raising the limit is mechanically easy: whoever makes a block may nudge it by up to a thousandth, and during 2025 it went from 30 to 60 million that way. But every unit of gas is work that every node repeats, and often state that every node keeps. By one measurement the state has been growing about three times as fast at 60 million as it did at 30. The limit is really a decision about who can still afford to run a node.

Gas says how much work a transaction is. It does not say what a unit of gas costs, or who gets in when more transactions arrive than a block can hold.

Bidding for space in a block

A block holds so much gas and no more, and on a busy day far more than that is waiting. Something has to decide who gets in. For its first six years Ethereum used an old answer, an auction. Every transaction named a gas price, the ether it would pay per unit of gas, and all of it went to the miner. Miners filled their blocks from the top. Below you are one sender among many. Your first transaction goes out by itself. Change your offer and send again:

You are bidding blind. Offer less than the crowd and you wait, perhaps for a long time. Offer more to be safe and you pay more than you needed to, because you pay what you bid. When demand rises the price that gets in changes from block to block, and a good guess a minute ago is a stuck transaction now. Wallets guessed on their users' behalf, and guessed high.

Here are gas prices year by year, through the auction years and after them:

In the auction years, up to 2021, the yearly average moved between 16 and 105 gwei, and single days went far beyond: 538 gwei on a day in September 2020. Even a mild case, a craze for collectible cats in December 2017, more than doubled the price within a week. The last bars belong to later sections. The trouble is less the level than the jumps: nobody knew the right bid.

A price set by the protocol

In August 2021 the auction was replaced. Under the new rule each block has one price per unit of gas, the base fee, which every transaction in it must pay, and that price is computed from the block before. Blocks were given a target, half of their limit. Change how full the left-hand block is:

If the block was exactly at its target the base fee stays where it was. Completely full, twice the target: up by an eighth. Empty: down by an eighth. In between, in proportion. That is the whole rule. Notice what a full block means now. It is no longer the normal state of things. It is a signal that demand is above what the chain can sustain.

One block moves the fee a little. The effect comes from repetition. Below, users keep arriving, each with a limit on what they will pay. Raise demand and wait a few blocks:

For a few blocks they fill to the brim. The slack between target and limit is what lets a sudden crowd in at once. Meanwhile the base fee climbs an eighth per block, a rate that doubles it in six blocks, until enough users find it too dear. Then blocks settle at half full again, at the new price. Nobody bid. The fee found the level at which demand meets the target, and a wallet can read it from the last block.

A sender now sets two numbers: a max fee, the most they will pay per unit of gas, and a small tip for the block producer, whoever makes the block: a miner in those years, a validator now. The tip (officially the priority fee) is the producer's reason to include a transaction at all, and to prefer it when a block is full. Move the three sliders:

The sender is charged the base fee plus the tip, not the max fee. The max is a ceiling that lets a transaction ride out a rise; whatever lies under it unused is never taken. If the base fee climbs past the max, the transaction waits. And the base fee is burned: it is paid to nobody, and that ether stops existing. The reason is defensive. If block producers received the base fee they could stuff their own blocks with empty transactions, drive it up, and collect. The tip is all they get. For Alice's transfer on our chain: 0.00021 ether burned, 0.000021 ether tipped.

The rule is simple enough to check by hand against the real chain. Here are three stretches of real blocks:

In the first minutes of the new rule nearly every block was full, and the base fee climbs from 1 gwei an eighth at a time. On 1 May 2022 the same staircase reaches 8,629 gwei in one block, the highest base fee ever recorded (the average gas price paid over that whole day was 475), before demand gives up. An ordinary minute in November 2026: about a tenth of a gwei, nudging up and down. In each, the next fee is exactly what the rule says.

What the rule did not do is make Ethereum cheap. Fees are high when demand exceeds capacity, and no pricing rule adds capacity. It made fees predictable and ended the overpaying.

Ether destroyed

Burning has a consequence for the currency as a whole. New ether is created, or issued, to reward those who secure the chain, as later sections will show, and ether is destroyed in every block. Set the base fee and see which wins:

Issuance does not depend on how busy the chain is. The burn depends on nothing else. At today's rate of issuance the two balance at a base fee of about 14 gwei. In September 2022 issuance was cut sharply, a story for a later section, and between then and April 2024 the supply of ether shrank by about 458,000. Since then fees have collapsed, for reasons this page will reach, and the supply is growing again by a little under 1% a year. In all, about 4.6 million ether have been burned.

The price is settled. Two things are not. Which transactions go into a block, and in what order, is still entirely up to whoever makes the block: hold on to that. And every block now changes a state of nearly 300 million accounts. How does anyone check the result?

One hash for the whole state

After every block each node holds a new state: nearly 300 million accounts and more than a billion storage cells at the last count, in May 2025. Two nodes should be able to confirm that their states are identical without comparing them entry by entry, and a block should be able to say, in a few bytes, which state it leads to. One hash of everything would do, if it did not mean rehashing everything after every change.

The way out is to hash in a tree. Hash each entry. Hash those hashes in pairs, then the results in pairs, until one hash is left: the root. Tap an account to change its balance, or change Bob's:

Four hashes out of fifteen were recomputed: the entry's own and the three above it. With eight entries the saving is small. With 300 million it is the difference between a few dozen hashes and 300 million. And yet the root still depends on every entry: change any one and the root changes. This is a Merkle tree.

The tree has a second use, and it is the more valuable one. Suppose you know only the root, and someone tells you Bob's balance. Step through how they prove it:

Bob's entry and three hashes, one neighbour for each level, let you recompute the path to the root for yourself. If your result equals the root you already trust, the claim is true, because nobody can find a different entry that leads to the same root without breaking the hash function. A false claim ends at a different root. That handful of hashes is a proof: three for eight entries, thirty for a billion.

Finding an account in the tree

A real state is not a fixed row of eight. Accounts turn up at arbitrary addresses, and a node must find any of them quickly. So Ethereum lays its tree out by the key itself: read the key as hex digits, and at each level take the branch that the next digit names. Build one from four short keys:

Keys that begin alike share a path and part where they first differ, at a junction with 16 places, one for each hex digit. A run of shared digits with no parting is folded into one connector to save levels. A tree laid out like this is a trie. Ethereum's is a Merkle tree at the same time: each junction is known by the hash of its contents, and its contents include the hashes of its children.

Now the real thing at toy size. The state is one trie, keyed by the hash of each address (hashed, so that nobody can choose addresses that pile up into long, slow paths). An account's place in it never moves, which is the fixed place the section on accounts promised. Apply Alice's two transactions to it:

The transfer changed two leaves and the junction above them. The token transfer shows the nesting: each contract's storage is a trie of its own, and its root is one of the four fields of the contract's account. So a change to one storage cell travels up the storage trie, into the account, up the state trie, and ends in a single 32-byte state root. That root is written into the header of every block, the block's short summary. Two nodes that computed the same root after a block hold identical states, down to the last cell.

Trust without a copy

The proof now works on the whole of Ethereum's state. A phone cannot hold the state, but it can hold the headers of blocks, which are small. Step through a question to a server it has no reason to trust:

The answer comes with the junctions along the path, and the phone checks each against the hash its parent holds, starting from the state root in the header. A lying server is caught at the first one that does not fit. A device that works this way is a light client. How it knows that a header belongs to the real chain is a question about who makes blocks. The answer comes with the validators' signatures. For a real account the path is about seven levels deep and the proof about 3 kilobytes.

That size has a cause, and it is the 16:

With 16 children per junction, a proof has to supply 15 neighbouring hashes at every level. A tree with two children per junction is deeper but needs one hash per level, and its proofs are several times smaller. Ethereum's researchers want to move the state into such a tree, so that one day a block could carry the proofs for everything it touches, and a node could check it while holding no state at all. As of late 2026 that is a draft, with no date.

Our chain now has everything a block needs: transactions, a machine to run them, a price, and a root to check the result. The blocks themselves are still handed out by burning electricity.

Retiring the miners

The section on mining ended with two debts. Here is the bill. Proof of work buys security by making blocks expensive, and somebody pays the expense. Compare what it cost with what replaced it, proof of stake, which the coming sections explain:

About 13,000 new ether a day went to miners, against about 1,700 a day to their replacements just after the switch. The electricity is harder to pin down: estimates for the last years of mining run from 21 to about 44 terawatt-hours a year, the scale of a whole country, and press reports quote figures twice as high. One estimate puts the replacement at 0.0026 terawatt-hours a year, and even the most cautious finds a saving of more than 99.8%.

The third pair is the weakness we met before, with a price on it: on a chain with little hash power of its own, an attack costs what it costs to rent some.

Ethereum's founders meant to leave proof of work from the beginning, and they built a timer into the chain to force the matter. An extra term in the difficulty, the difficulty bomb, doubles every 100,000 blocks. For a long time it is too small to notice. Move the chain forward:

The difficulty rule lowers the difficulty only after a slow block. So once the bomb's term is as large as one ordinary adjustment, the rule can cancel it only by letting every block come slower: in this model 16 seconds, 20, then nearly 40. (On the real chain the worst day, in 2017, averaged 30.)

The only escape is to upgrade every node, either to the replacement or, when the replacement was not ready, to a version with the bomb pushed back. That happened six times between 2017 and 2022. The founders had allowed sixteen months. It took seven years. The bomb could not force the switch. What it did was make doing nothing impossible: every delay needed every node operator to act.

The replacement was built alongside. On 1 December 2020 a second chain started up, carrying no transactions at all: the Beacon chain. Its blocks are made by participants who have locked up ether, in a way the next sections explain. For almost two years it ran in parallel, and nothing on the old chain depended on it. Then the two were joined. Step through the join:

Nothing restarted. Accounts, contracts and history carried on, and block 15,537,394 follows block 15,537,393. What changed is where a block comes from. The last one was mined. The next arrived 17 seconds later as the cargo of a Beacon chain block, on 15 September 2022. The switch was set to fire at a total amount of work, not at a block number or a date, because a branch built with little hash power can reach any block number, but not a given total of work. This is the Merge.

Here is the block's header just before and just after:

The fields of mining are still there, and empty: difficulty 0, nonce 0, no uncles. One has a new job and carries a random number supplied by the Beacon chain. The miners lost their use overnight. All the other chains their machines could mine took in less than a third of the hash power.

"The cargo of a Beacon chain block." We have swapped the lottery for something we have not looked at. How does a chain with no miners decide who makes the next block?

Stake instead of work

Proof of work made cheating expensive by making everything expensive. Proof of stake looks for a lottery ticket that costs nothing to hold and a great deal to abuse. The ticket is ether, locked inside the protocol. It earns a little while its owner follows the rules, and it can be destroyed if its owner is caught breaking them.

Each such lock, together with the key that will vote for it, is a validator, and the locked ether is its stake. The person or company that runs it is its operator, and one operator may run thousands. Time on this chain is cut into slots of 12 seconds, and 32 slots make an epoch of 6.4 minutes. Suppose Alice has saved up 32 ether. Follow her as she becomes a validator, and later leaves:

She sends 32 ether and a new public key to a contract, and the validator that the key belongs to joins the set after a queue. The queue is deliberate. Only 256 ether's worth of new stake is let in per epoch, about 57,600 ether a day, and leaving is rationed the same way, so that the set of validators changes only slowly. On 17 November 2026 some 896,000 ether was waiting to get in: a wait of fifteen and a half days.

Who proposes, who votes

In each slot exactly one validator makes a block. It is that slot's proposer, and it is chosen by a draw. A validator's stake starts at 32 ether and may be as large as 2,048. Let the draw run, then raise one validator's balance:

A validator's chance is in proportion to its stake. One with 2,048 ether proposes 64 times as often as one with 32, exactly as if it were 64 validators.

The draw needs randomness that every node agrees on and nobody controls, and there is nowhere outside to get it. So the proposers make it. Each one stirs into a running mix its signature over the number of the epoch. It is a signature of the kind the next section opens, which has exactly one valid value, so that only that proposer can produce it and even it cannot choose it, and the mix that picks an epoch's proposers was fixed two epochs earlier. One small lever remains: the last proposer of an epoch can withhold its block and so change the mix, at the cost of the block.

The other validators are not idle. Every one of them votes, once in every epoch, on the chain as it sees it. To spread the work they are shuffled into groups, one group for each slot:

Our 12 fall into four slots of three. Each validator votes in exactly one slot per epoch, and it cannot choose which, so a slot's voters are a fair sample of everybody. The voters of a slot are its attesters, and they are organised in committees. On the real chain about 784,700 validators are dealt out over 32 slots: about 24,500 to a slot, in 64 committees. A committee's votes travel in a channel of their own, which splits the traffic. A vote says, in effect, "this is the chain as I see it". What exactly it contains can wait two sections.

Carrot

Validators are paid in new ether for votes that arrive on time and agree with what the chain goes on to decide, and for proposing. How much depends on how many of them there are:

The rate falls as the stake grows: at best 5.26% a year with 10 million ether staked, and about 2.5% with today's 44.6 million. The total issued grows only with the square root of the stake, so four times the stake costs twice as much. The curve pays the first stakers well and each newcomer a little less. In ordinary times a validator that is offline loses roughly what it would have earned, and nothing worse. Being offline is not an attack. (One exceptional regime is harsher on absence. It comes with finality.)

Stick

An attack is signing two things that contradict each other, such as two different blocks for the same slot. No network fault can cause that. It takes the key, and the two signatures together are the proof. Make validator 5 do it:

Anyone who sees both signatures can put them in a block, and the protocol does the rest. The validator is fined and put out of the set: this is slashing. The fine has two parts, and the second is the interesting one: three times the share of all stake that was slashed within the same few weeks.

Alone, the fine is less than a hundredth of an ether (the five weeks of forced absence that follow cost several times more): a lone fault is treated as a mistake. If a third of all stake is caught together, each slashed validator loses everything, because that is no accident. Nearly all real slashings have been of the first kind: an operator running one key on two machines.

Here are six years of validators and their stake:

From 21,063 validators in December 2020 to over a million in 2024, each with 32 ether. Then the count falls while the stake goes on rising. Since May 2025 a single validator may hold up to 2,048 ether, and large operators have been merging theirs. The reason for allowing that comes at the end of the next section.

Every validator signs a vote in every epoch, and every vote has to be carried in a block and checked by every node.

Many signatures in one

Count them. About 784,700 validators each sign one vote per epoch, which comes to about 24,500 signatures in every 12-second slot. Here is what that weighs:

At 96 bytes apiece a slot's signatures come to 2.35 megabytes, many times the size of the block they are voting on, and every node would have to check each one. Switch aggregation on. Each committee's votes are added up, and committees that voted alike are folded together again: for a slot's identical votes a block carries one signature of 96 bytes and a strip of bits saying whose it is. The signatures of the earlier section cannot do this: two of them added together are not a signature of anything. Validators use a different kind, called BLS after its inventors, and it rests on one new tool.

The tool

This part leans on the curve points of "Inside a signature": points that can be added, and multiplied by a number. The tool is a pairing. It takes one point from each of two groups of curve points and returns a value, and it has one remarkable property: a multiplier can be moved from either point to the other without changing the result. Try it in a toy:

Whether a multiplies the first point, or the second, or both multipliers sit on one side, the value is the same. That lets a checker test whether two hidden multiplications used the same number without ever seeing the number. A note on honesty: in my toy a point is written as its multiplier modulo 31 and the pairing multiplies the two, so nothing is hidden at all. A real pairing, on a curve named BLS12-381, gives the same equalities while keeping each multiplier as hard to find as a private key.

A BLS signature is a single multiplication. Step through one being made and checked:

The validator's secret key is a number (the same idea as a private key), and its public key is that number times a fixed point P. To sign, it turns the vote into a point H of the other group and multiplies H by the secret key. The checker computes two pairings: P with the signature, and the public key with H. In both, the secret key appears once as a multiplier, on opposite sides, so the two values are equal. Test the signature against another vote and H differs, and so do the values.

Adding up

Now the reason for the detour. Below, eight validators have signed the same vote. Tap any of them to leave it out or put it back:

Add the chosen signatures and you have one signature. Add the same validators' public keys and you have one key. The check passes on the two sums, because a pairing treats sums as it treats multipliers: the pairing of a sum is the pairings of its parts, combined. What held for each signer holds for all of them added up.

The result is an aggregate: 96 bytes, plus the strip of bits that tells a checker which public keys to add. Get one bit wrong and the sum of keys is wrong, and the check fails. However many signed, checking takes two pairings and some additions. A validator's signed vote is called an attestation, and what a block carries is this: a vote, a strip of bits, one aggregate signature.

There is one trap. Here are an honest validator and an attacker, about to sign together:

The attacker announced a public key made by subtracting the honest validator's key from its own. Added up, the two announced keys cancel down to the attacker's real key, so the attacker's signature alone passes as a signature by both. The defence is to demand proof: before a key is admitted its owner must sign the key itself, which the attacker cannot do for a key whose secret it does not know. Every validator's deposit carries such a signature.

Even so, every validator is one more bit in the strip, one more public key to add, one more vote to pass around the network. That is why, since May 2025, an operator with many validators may merge them into fewer and larger ones.

One more use, owed since the section on the state: a panel of 512 validators, redrawn about once a day, signs the header of every block with one aggregate signature. That is how a light client knows a header is genuine without following the chain.

Votes are now cheap to carry and to count. Votes for what?

Which block is the head

Proposers are drawn, attesters are shuffled, and their votes can be added up. The first thing they vote on is which block the chain currently ends with. That sounds like no question at all: the newest one. But blocks get lost, arrive late, or are held back on purpose, and two honest validators can disagree about which block is the newest. Start with one slot and its clock:

The proposer publishes at the start of the slot. As soon as that block arrives, and four seconds in at the latest, the slot's attesters vote for the newest block they have seen. Usually that is the new one: on the real network of 2025 the typical block arrived in under two seconds. A block that takes five seconds finds its voters gone, having voted for its parent. Eight seconds in, the votes are aggregated, and the next slot's block will carry them.

A vote says more than "this block". Here is one opened up:

Three statements under one signature. The first names the head: the block this validator takes to be the end of the chain. The other two link a pair of checkpoints, and belong to the next section. The head vote is the one we need now.

Follow the votes

Given everyone's head votes, here is how a node finds the head. Start from the last block that all validators already agree on (the next section says which that is). If one block follows it, step to that. If several do, add up for each of them the stake of every validator whose latest vote is for that block or for anything built on it, and step to the heaviest. Repeat until nothing follows. Drag a validator to change its vote:

From J, the branch through B has five validators behind it, one on B and two each on D and E, against four on the branch through A. So the first step is to B. D and E then tie at two validators each, and a tie is settled by comparing the two blocks' hashes.

Only a validator's latest vote counts, so voting often gains nothing, and a vote for a block also supports every block before it. Move E's two votes to C and the path swings to the upper branch. This rule is the chain's fork choice. Its formal name is LMD-GHOST, an abbreviation of the rule you have just read: latest messages, heaviest subtree.

A quick test of intuition. Decide which of these two tips is the head, then press Reveal:

The shorter branch. Proof of work left behind the slogan that the longest chain wins (strictly, the one with the most work in it). Here length counts for nothing. A branch weighs what the stake voting for it weighs.

When it goes wrong

The rule earns its keep when a block is late. Step through four slots:

The block of slot 2 missed its voters. The proposer of slot 3 finds a head with almost nothing behind it. By the plain rule that head would still stand, being the only block after its parent. So there is an explicit exception: a proposer may pass over a head that arrived late and has almost no votes, and build on the block before it.

The late block is dropped (under proof of work we called such a block stale): it is left off the chain, and its transactions go back among the pending ones to be included again. In 2025 about one block in a thousand was dropped, some eight a day, most of them for arriving late, and a later sample found nearly two in a thousand. That is the system working. It is also a block that was part of the chain and then was not.

Lateness can be faked. An attacker who is the proposer of one slot can keep its block and its votes hidden, then release them at the right moment to push the next, honest block off the chain. Set the attacker's share and run it:

The honest block has had no time to collect votes, so the attacker's hidden votes outweigh it: a tenth of a slot's voters is enough. The countermeasure is a head start. A block that arrives on time in its own slot is counted, for that slot, as if 40% of the slot's stake had already voted for it. With that boost the hidden votes must outweigh it, and this simple attack needs more than two fifths of a slot's voters.

The boost was added in 2022, after researchers showed that such attacks worked with very little stake. It raised the bar without closing the door: subtler variants are estimated to work from about 7% when the network favours the attacker.

The head is the validators' best answer so far, and as the last two figures show, it can still change. Someone handing over goods needs to know when it cannot.

When a block is final

Under proof of work a payment was only ever probably settled, and the head rule of the last section is no firmer: it follows the latest votes wherever they go. Blocks that cannot be undone come from the other two statements in every vote.

Once per epoch, the first block of the epoch is singled out as a checkpoint. (If that slot is empty, the last block before it serves.) Each vote names two checkpoints: a source, the newest checkpoint the validator regards as agreed, and a target, the checkpoint of the current epoch. Read it as "I have moved on from there to here". Step through three epochs:

When votes from at least two thirds of all stake name the same pair, the target is justified. When the very next checkpoint is justified as well, with the first as its source, the first is finalized: it is final, and so is every block before it. Two rounds, each needing two thirds.

Why two? After the first round two thirds have voted for the checkpoint, but none of them yet knows that the others did. In the second round two thirds name it as their source: they have seen it justified, and the rules below bind them to build from it. The head rule of the last section starts its walk at the newest justified checkpoint, and never leaves a finalized one behind.

A real epoch is 6.4 minutes, so a checkpoint is final 12.8 minutes after it appears, and a transaction waits 13 to 19 minutes depending on where in an epoch it landed. Two thirds means two thirds of the stake, not of the validators. Votes are weighed.

Below two thirds

What happens when two thirds cannot be reached? Take validators offline:

With five of the twelve offline the bars fall short, and nothing new becomes final. But blocks keep coming, with gaps where an absent validator should have proposed. That is a choice. Some other designs halt outright when a third of their participants vanish. Ethereum keeps the chain moving and suspends only its promise of finality. It has been tested: in May 2023 a fault in some validators' software stalled finality twice, for about four epochs and then about nine, and blocks never stopped.

Still, a chain that cannot finalize is not one to rely on for long, and the missing validators might never come back. So while finality is stalled a second mechanism goes to work on them:

The balances of absent validators drain away, slowly at first and faster the longer the stall lasts. Their share of the total shrinks until those present hold two thirds again, and finality resumes. With 34% offline that takes about four and a half days; with 40%, two weeks. This is the inactivity leak, and it is how the chain recovers from a catastrophe, such as a whole region going dark, without anybody having to decide anything.

Why final means final

Finality rests on a promise that validators make by voting, and the promise is enforced by slashing. Two kinds of contradiction are forbidden. Vote A below is fixed. Move vote B around it:

A validator may not cast two different votes for the same target epoch. And it may not cast a vote whose span reaches around another of its votes, such as one from 1 to 6 around one from 2 to 5, or sits inside one. Either contradiction can be proven from the two signed votes alone, and either is punished as in the section on validators.

Those two rules give finality its teeth. Suppose two conflicting checkpoints were both finalized. Count who voted:

Each needed two thirds, and two groups of two thirds overlap in at least one third. The validators in the overlap voted for both histories, and it can be shown that their votes break one of the two rules. So a finalized block can be undone only if at least a third of all stake signs provable contradictions and is destroyed for it. On today's Ethereum a third of the stake is about 14.9 million ether, some 27 billion dollars at the price of the day I am writing. Final does not mean that reverting is impossible. It means reverting has a known, enormous and automatic price.

Here are the thresholds together. Move the attacker's share:

A third of the stake can stop finality by keeping silent, and is then drained by the leak. More than half can steer the head, which lets it delay transactions and drop recent blocks, but it cannot finalize anything alone. Two thirds can finalize what it likes. Against that the last defence lies outside the protocol: the people who use the chain can agree to run software that disregards the attacker's stake, as they once did for another reason in 2016.

The chain now decides what is settled. One power has been growing quietly through the last four sections, though. The proposer of a slot decides which transactions its block contains, and in what order, and that turns out to be worth money.

The order is worth money

Go back to the moment before a block. Alice has signed her transaction, and it has to reach whoever proposes next. She gives it to one node, and nodes pass it on. Watch it spread, or send another:

Soon every node holds the transaction among its pending ones, in its pool (the usual name is mempool). There is no single pool. Each node has its own, in whatever order things reached it. And there is no privacy: a transaction sent this way is public from the moment it leaves until a block fixes its place. (Many senders now avoid the public pool by handing transactions privately to the specialists of the next section.) That is a matter of seconds, which is plenty for the marked node. It belongs to a searcher, someone who reads every pending transaction looking for one to profit from.

Here is what that visibility means in the plainest case. Make a guess first:

The bot does not need to understand what Alice's transaction does. It tries out every pending transaction with its own address in place of the sender's, and when the copy would make money it sends the copy with a better offer. The two engineers who described this in 2020 were trying to rescue about 12,000 dollars' worth of tokens from a contract that anyone could empty. They lost them to such a bot, and compared the pool to a dark forest.

Copying is the crude way to profit. The subtle way is through order. Take an exchange contract: it holds a pile of ether and a pile of tokens and trades with anyone, at a price set by the ratio of the piles (another page of this site takes one apart). Every trade moves its price. Change the order of two trades:

Alice sells 5 ether. If nothing runs before her she receives 9,950.25 dollar tokens. If someone else's sale runs first, the price has already fallen and the same 5 ether fetch less. Same transactions, same block, a different outcome, by order alone. And the order inside a block is whatever its producer chooses.

The sandwich

A searcher who sees Alice's pending sale can arrange that on purpose, with a transaction of its own on each side of hers:

The searcher sells just before Alice and pushes the price down. Alice's sale goes through at the worse price and pushes it further. The searcher buys back just after, for less than it sold. Alice's only protection is the limit she set: her transaction cancels itself if she would receive more than, say, 1% below the quoted amount. So the searcher pushes her exactly to that limit. At 1% she receives 9,850.75 tokens where she expected 9,950.25, and the searcher ends 0.05 ether ahead, about 100 dollars, in a toy with no trading fee. A looser limit is a larger gift.

What can be earned by choosing the order of transactions has a name: MEV, maximal extractable value. The sandwich is its ugliest form. Much of the rest is harmless, such as buying on one exchange and selling on another until their prices agree.

The fight for first place

A sandwich works only if the searcher's first transaction lands immediately before Alice's. Under the old auction, place in a block went by gas price. So the searchers' programs, their bots, fought for it in the open. Step through one fight over a single prize:

Each bot can see the other's offer and beats it, by at least a tenth or an eighth each time (the smallest raise the node software of the day would accept), again and again in the seconds before the block. The block then includes both. The winner takes the prize. The loser's transaction finds nothing, fails, and still pays for its gas. Researchers who recorded these auctions for a study published in 2019 counted more than forty bids from each of two bots within thirteen seconds. Everyone else paid as well, in block space taken by failed transactions and in gas prices bid up for all.

Early in 2021 the fight moved out of sight. Run the same contest both ways:

A searcher no longer shouts bids across the public pool. It sends a sealed bundle, its transactions in the order it wants (other people's pending ones included, such as Alice's sale between the searcher's two) with a payment attached, through a relay, a go-between we will meet again, to the miners who have signed up. A miner includes the best-paying bundle whole, or not at all. Losers pay nothing and take up no space.

The scheme came from a group called Flashbots. By its own count, miners holding 3 to 4% of the hash power accepted bundles in January 2021 and over 80% by mid-May. Order had become something a block producer sells in private.

Sealed bundles need a block producer who can be trusted not to open one and steal the idea. A few well-known groups of miners could be held to that. Since 2022 the producers are hundreds of thousands of anonymous validators, each for 12 seconds at a time.

Who really builds the block

Getting the most out of a block is by now a specialist's trade: collect bundles from searchers, try thousands of combinations, strike private deals for transactions. If validators had to do that themselves, the largest and best equipped would earn the most, the rest would fall behind, and the stake would gather in a few hands. The way out is to split the job in two.

Specialists called builders assemble blocks and bid for the right to have them proposed. The proposer's only task is to take the highest bid. The difficulty is the handover. If the builder shows its block, the proposer can copy the contents and keep the profit. If it does not, the proposer is asked to sign something it has never seen. Today a go-between settles it. Step through a slot:

The relay takes blocks from builders and shows the proposer only a header and a bid. The proposer signs the header, which commits it to that block (signing a second one would be slashable), without having seen a single transaction in it. Only then does the relay publish the block.

In one week of October 2026 nine blocks in ten were made this way. The bids are modest, a median of 0.0058 ether against the roughly 0.05 ether that the protocol itself pays for proposing, but they are the proposer's share of whatever its block was worth, earned without any skill. The tips and everything else the block yields go to the builder, who pays the proposer the bid.

All of it hangs on the relay doing its part. On 3 April 2023 one did not. Run the slot with a dishonest proposer:

A signed header is normally a binding promise: publishing any other block for that slot gets the proposer slashed. This proposer signed a header that was deliberately invalid, one the network would never accept. The relay did not check, took the signature for the usual promise, and released the block's contents. The block it had been keeping could not be published under that header, so nothing competed with the proposer's own.

Holding other people's trades in the clear, the proposer rebuilt the block so that those trades worked in its own favour. The losses were about 20 million dollars by the count of the relay software's maintainers and about 25 million by that of prosecutors. Those who lost were sandwich bots. The proposer was slashed for its two signatures, which cost it 1 ether at the time. The repair was for relays to verify what was signed and to publish the block themselves before revealing anything.

Few builders

Here is who built the blocks that came through relays, about nine in ten of all blocks, on one day in November 2026:

One builder made more than half of them, and the first three made four fifths. The relays are fewer still, and their first three carried 86% of the blocks. Set this beside some 784,700 validators, and you see the bargain that was struck. Proposing stays open to anyone with 32 ether and a well-equipped desktop computer, because it no longer takes skill. Building is concentrated. The bet is that this is safe as long as builders cannot do the most harmful thing in their power, which is to keep transactions out.

That has been tried. In August 2022 the United States placed a set of Ethereum contracts under sanctions, and several relays began to refuse blocks that touched them. What does that do to a transaction? Set the share of blocks that filter:

It delays the transaction. A filtered transaction waits for the first slot whose block comes from somewhere that does not filter. At the peak, in October 2022, by one widely quoted count 94.8% of the blocks delivered by relays came through filtering ones. Not every block came through a relay, though, and the waits that were measured were short: in November 2022 a sanctioned transaction waited 29 seconds on average, against 9 for others.

By November 2026 the share is about 12%, and at that share a filtered transaction should wait hardly more than one slot. So long as some proposers take unfiltered blocks, or build their own, nothing is kept out for good. But "so long as some" is thin ground for a network that is meant to be neutral.

Into the protocol
