Two changes are meant to settle this. Neither is live as I write, in November 2026. The first moves the handover between builder and proposer into the rules themselves, with no relay to trust. Step through the slot as it is planned:

The proposer's block now holds a builder's signed bid in place of transactions. Builders, under these rules, put up a stake of their own, and the amount of the bid is set aside out of it. Once the proposer's block has the votes of 60% of the slot's attesters, the proposer is paid whatever the builder does next. The builder has until the middle of the slot to reveal the transactions, and a separate panel of 512 validators votes on whether it did.

A builder that reveals nothing has paid for an empty slot. This is scheduled for an upgrade named Glamsterdam, which is running on test networks and has no date for the main one. It removes the need to trust a relay. It does not make builders more numerous.

The second change takes away a builder's power to exclude. Switch the lists on:

In every slot sixteen validators each publish a short list of transactions they can see waiting. Attesters then refuse to vote for a block that leaves out a listed transaction which would have fitted. A builder could make every block there is and still not keep Alice out, provided one of the sixteen is honest. This inclusion list is planned for the upgrade after Glamsterdam.

However a block is built, one block every 12 seconds holds 60 million gas, and we saw what that comes to: about 22 transactions a second. The world does not fit.

A second layer

Twenty-two transactions a second, for everybody, because every node executes every transaction and the limit has to suit the weakest node worth keeping. Raising the limit moves that number a little. Since 2020 Ethereum's main answer has been to move the execution somewhere else.

A rollup is a separate chain with blocks of its own, usually run by a single operator, that leans on Ethereum for what it cannot supply itself. Ethereum is then called layer 1 and the rollup layer 2. Compare a thousand transfers done both ways:

On the left every Ethereum node does all the work: 21 million gas. On the right one computer, the rollup's sequencer, executes the transfers. Ethereum receives only their bytes, in a batch, and one state root that claims the result. Its nodes store and order the batch and execute nothing: about 4.4 million gas if the bytes are posted as ordinary transaction data, less once the batch is compressed, and far less by the route of the next section. The bytes are the point. With them, anyone can re-execute the batch and find out whether the claimed root is true.

Follow some money in and out:

Alice's ether never leaves layer 1. It sits in a bridge contract, and the rollup keeps a balance for her. A payment on the rollup is confirmed by the sequencer at once and reaches layer 1 in the next batch. To leave, Bob shows the bridge his rollup balance with a proof against a state root, the kind of proof we met with the trie.

And if the sequencer ignores Alice, she can post her transaction on layer 1 herself, and the rollup's rules oblige it to include it within a day. The sequencer can delay and reorder. It cannot forge, and it cannot lock anyone in, provided the bridge accepts only true state roots. Everything hangs on that proviso.

Two ways to trust a root

The first way is to accept a root unless somebody objects. Rollups that work so are called optimistic. An objection has to be settled by a contract on layer 1, which cannot re-run a whole batch. It does not need to. Play the challenger:

The two parties agree at the start and disagree at the end, so somewhere there is a first step on which they differ, and halving finds it: ten rounds for 1,024 steps, thirty for a billion. Layer 1 then executes that single step, one instruction, and whoever was wrong loses a deposit. This is a fraud proof. One honest challenger is enough, but that challenger needs time, even if builders try to keep its transactions out of blocks, and so the window for objections is about a week.

The second way is to prove every root correct before accepting it. A validity proof is a short piece of data showing that a stated computation on stated inputs gives a stated output. How one is made is beyond this page. What matters here is its shape:

A proof is a few hundred bytes and costs layer 1 a few hundred thousand gas to check, about 270,000 for one common kind, whether it covers one transaction or ten thousand. Spread over a large batch, certainty costs next to nothing per transaction. The expensive part is producing the proof, which the rollup does on its own machines. Rollups of this kind are often called ZK rollups, ZK for zero-knowledge. The name comes from the mathematics behind the proofs and does not mean their transactions are private. With rare exceptions they are not.

The difference shows when money leaves:

From an optimistic rollup a withdrawal waits out the window for objections. From a validity rollup it waits only for the next proof to be accepted, a matter of hours.

How much to believe

"Secured by Ethereum" is every rollup's selling line. How true it is depends on the rollup:

The stages are a public scoring by a group that tracks rollups. Stage 0: the essential machinery exists, but the operators could still take the money. (A contract's code cannot be edited, but a contract can be written to pass every call on to another contract whose address its owners may change: the delegate call from the section on the EVM. Every large rollup's contracts can be replaced this way today.) Stage 1: only a large majority of a security council, a named group of people who hold keys to the contracts, could. Stage 2: the council can step in only for a bug that is proven on the chain.

Of the eight largest rollups five are at stage 1 and three at stage 0. One of the largest, Arbitrum One, ran for three and a half years before fraud proofs were opened to everyone; until then only an approved list could challenge. This section has described what a rollup can be. The stage says how far a particular one has come.

One cost long dominated a rollup's bill: the bytes it posts to layer 1.

Cheap space for data

Until March 2024 rollups posted their batches as call data, the same bytes that carry the arguments of a call. Call data is priced for what it is: bytes that contracts can read while they run, and that nodes keep as part of the chain's history. A rollup's batch is read by no contract, and it is needed only until anyone who cares has checked it.

So Ethereum added a second kind of space to a block, made for this: the blob. A blob is 131,072 bytes that travel with a block and that the EVM cannot read. Compare what the same bytes cost each way:

On the day of my sample, a blob's worth of bytes cost 0.00066 ether as call data and under a millionth of an ether as a blob. The gap exists because blobs do not compete with transactions for gas. They have a limit per block of their own, and a price of their own. All the blobs ever posted have cost their senders 4,748 ether together; as call data the same bytes would have cost 619,308. This, along with the larger gas limit of 2025, is why fees have been so low lately, and why the burn of ether fell with them.

The price of blobs follows a rule you already know. Change how many are wanted:

There is a target of 14 blobs per block and a maximum of 21, and a blob base fee that rises while blocks carry more than the target and falls while they carry fewer. One thing was added in December 2025: a reserve price, one sixteenth of the ordinary base fee, below which the blob fee stops falling. Without it the blob fee had often sat at practically zero, where it steered nothing.

Here is the life of one blob, day by day:

The block keeps only a 48-byte commitment to the blob. The bytes travel beside the block, and nodes are obliged to keep them and hand them out for about 18 days, long enough for anyone who needs a rollup's batch to fetch it. After that a node may delete them. A contract can see a hash of a blob's commitment and never the contents.

Committing to a blob

A commitment has to tie the sender to the exact bytes. A tree of hashes would do that, and could even prove single pieces, as we saw. Ethereum wants two things more: a proof that stays 48 bytes however large the blob, and a guarantee that all the pieces of a blob lie on one polynomial, which the next section will need. So its commitment treats the data as a polynomial. (What follows leans on the curve points of "Inside a signature" and the pairing of "Many signatures in one".) First see that nothing is lost that way. Drag the four values:

Four numbers fix exactly one polynomial of degree three, and its graph gives the four numbers back. The same holds modulo 17, and modulo the very large prime that Ethereum uses, where the 4,096 numbers of a blob fix one polynomial.

Here is the task. Someone holding a blob has published its commitment. Later a checker, who holds only the commitment, wants one piece of the data. The holder, the prover, must answer with the value and with a short proof that this value really belongs to what was committed.

The commitment is the value of the polynomial at one secret number that nobody knows. Step through the toy:

Here is the idea. If the polynomial has the value 10 at x = 2, then subtracting 10 leaves a polynomial that is zero at 2, so it divides exactly by x − 2. The prover sends the value of the quotient at the secret number, and the checker multiplies back and compares. Claim the value 11, which is false: the division leaves a remainder, and nothing the prover can send will fit.

In the toy the secret number is in plain view. In reality nobody has it. What was published instead is a list of curve points: G times the secret, G times its square, G times its cube, and so on. From those anyone can work out a polynomial's value at the secret, as a curve point, without learning the secret, and the multiplying back happens inside a pairing, the tool from the validators' signatures.

One number is enough because two different polynomials of a blob's size agree at fewer than 4,096 numbers out of about 2²⁵⁵: if they agree at a number nobody could aim for, they are the same. Commitment and proof are 48 bytes each. The scheme is known by its inventors' initials, KZG.

"A secret number that nobody knows" needs an explanation. It was made by many people in turn:

Each contributor mixed in a secret number of their own and passed on only the hidden result. Whoever knows every contributor's number knows the secret and can forge proofs. If a single contributor destroyed theirs, nobody knows it. Ethereum's ceremony ran from January to August 2023 and took 141,416 contributions. The arrangement is called a trusted setup, and the trust it asks for is that not every one of them colluded.

Blobs made rollups cheap. They left one thing as it was. To be sure that a blob really was published, every node downloaded all of it, so the number of blobs per block was capped by what the slowest node could fetch.

Checking data without downloading it

A commitment proves what a blob contains. It does not prove that anybody ever published the contents, and that gap is serious. Below, a rollup's sequencer posts a batch. Withhold one piece, then let the challenger complain:

The sequencer posted a commitment and a state root and kept back a piece of the batch. Nobody can recompute the state, so nobody can show the root to be wrong, whatever it hides. And the keeping back cannot itself be proven to a contract: when the challenger complains, the sequencer produces the piece and looks innocent. An earlier plan for scaling Ethereum, called Plasma, was abandoned in good part over this. The publishing has to be witnessed at the time, by the nodes themselves, and an Ethereum node does refuse a block whose blobs it cannot get.

Downloading everything settles the matter and does not scale. The alternative begins with a trick the polynomial makes possible. Erase some pieces:

A polynomial fixed by four values can be evaluated at four more values of x. Now there are eight values, and any four of them determine the polynomial and with it all eight. Rebuild from whatever four you left. This stretching doubles the data and changes the withholder's problem completely. Hiding one piece is pointless, since the others rebuild it. To withhold anything, more than half has to be withheld.

And more than half is easy to notice. Set how much the block's producer hides (its builder, or a proposer building for itself) and how many pieces a checker asks for:

Ask for one piece at random: if more than half are hidden you hit a hole more than half the time. Ask for eight, and the chance that all eight happen to be there is under one in 256. With twenty it is under one in a million. A checker can be all but certain that the data is there after fetching a small part of it. This is sampling.

Ethereum has worked this way, in a first form, since December 2025. Change how many columns the producer publishes:

Every blob is stretched to twice its length and cut into 128 pieces, and the pieces with the same number, across all the blobs of a block, form a column. Each node fetches at least 8 of the 128 columns in every slot, and nodes whose validators hold more than 256 ether between them keep more. They are a fixed set worked out from the node's identity, not a fresh random draw, which is where the real system differs from the textbook picture above.

A node accepts a block only if its 8 columns arrive. If a producer publishes fewer than half the columns, so that the data cannot be rebuilt, a node is fooled only when all 8 of its columns are among the published ones. For columns picked at random that is fewer than 3 nodes in a thousand, and the rest of the network refuses the block. A producer can work out whom a given choice would fool, but it has to make one choice for the whole network, and even a clever choice deceives only a small minority.

Each column comes with a short proof, of the kind from the last section, that it belongs to the blobs the block committed to. Each node downloads a sixteenth of the stretched data, which is as many bytes as an eighth of the blobs themselves, and together the nodes hold all of it.

Here is what that bought:

For twenty-one months the maximum moved once, from 6 blobs per block to 9, because every increase cost every node bandwidth. Within five weeks of the change to columns it went to 15 and then to 21. In my sample of November 2026 about 5 blobs per block were in use, well under the target of 14. For the moment there is more room than demand.

That is the whole machine. What remains is to watch it handle one transfer.

One slot, start to finish

Piece by piece we have built something that must, in the end, run on an ordinary computer. Here is what a node is today. Step through one slot:

A node is two programs, written by different teams, that talk over a local connection. The consensus client follows the validators: slots, votes, the head, finality. The execution client holds the state and the pool and runs the EVM. Once a slot, the first asks the second either to build a block (unless a builder supplies one, as happens nine times in ten) or to check one.

The seam between them is the scar of the Merge: the execution client does the job of the old proof-of-work node, minus the mining. Each program exists in several independent versions, so that a fault in one of them does not take the network down.

And now the transfer from the top of the page, for the last time:

Alice's key multiplies a point on a curve. A sponge of 1,600 bits makes the number she signs. Nodes pass the transaction along. A builder gives it a place, and a proposer drawn by stake signs for the block. Every node's EVM recovers her address, checks her nonce, moves 1 ether, charges 21,000 gas and burns the base fee.

A trie yields a new state root. The slot's attesters vote, and their signatures add up into one. The votes choose the head, and two rounds of two thirds make it final. Bob has 3 ether. On the real chain it would have taken about a quarter of an hour and, at the prices of November 2026, half a cent.

Almost none of this was there in 2015, and little of it will stay as it is. Move through the upgrades:

The protocol has been changed more than twenty times, each time by node operators installing new software that switches rules at an agreed block or moment. Nobody can force an upgrade. Operators who refuse carry on under the old rules, as Ethereum Classic did. As I write, the next upgrade, Glamsterdam, is running on test networks and has been held back: its new gas prices turned out to break assumptions in contracts that are already deployed, and nobody can yet say when it reaches the main network. After it, inclusion lists are planned, and a slot of 10 seconds in place of 12 is being considered for the same upgrade.

Further out it is research, and should be called that: finality in seconds instead of a quarter of an hour, a state tree with two children per junction, nodes that check a short proof of a block instead of executing it, and signatures that a quantum computer could not forge. That last one matters to everything on this page that leans on curve points: transaction signatures, validators' aggregates and blob commitments would all fall to such a machine, while the hashes would stand.

Further reading

  • The Ethereum whitepaper, by Vitalik Buterin. The motivation in the author's own words: what Bitcoin's scripts could not do, and the first sketch of accounts, contracts and gas.
  • The execution specifications. The rules for transactions, gas and the state trie as short, readable Python. Every price on this page can be looked up there.
  • evm.codes. Every instruction of the EVM with its stack effect and its price, and a playground for running bytecode.
  • EIP-1559. The base fee, with its motivation in four bullet points and a complete reference implementation.
  • Upgrading Ethereum, by Ben Edgington. Proof of stake rule by rule, each with its reason and its history: rewards, slashing, the fork choice, finality, BLS signatures.
  • Ethereum is a Dark Forest, by Dan Robinson and Georgios Konstantopoulos. The story that makes the public pool's visibility concrete.
  • EIP-4844. Blobs, their fee rule and the reasoning behind them, in one document.
  • KZG polynomial commitments, by Dankrad Feist. The whole scheme on one page, for a reader comfortable with the toy version here.

Final words

You open a wallet, type an amount and press Send. You know now what the wallet does with your key, and why the transaction does not need to say who you are. You know why it waits, who can see it while it does, and who decides where it goes. You know what every node does with it, what it is charged and where the charge ends up. And you know what has to happen, twice, before taking it back would cost a third of everything staked.

Ethereum is often described as a world computer. It is a slow one, on purpose. Each part we added made it slower or dearer than a single machine would be, and each bought the same thing: one more question that nobody has to be trusted to answer.
